verdicts.note: Chief criminal deputy since 2018, in the office since 2011 [S4], 22 years a prosecutor [S6], the retiring prosecutor's endorsed successor running explicitly on experience and a no-learning-curve pitch [S1][S6]. Not an incumbent, but the long tenure and management role make her the maximal record case here; high is supported by three sources.

'Holding offenders accountable' and fighting for victims as top priority [S5], police-leader endorsements [S3], and no diversion or treatment proposals anywhere in the dossier. Her access-to-justice and reporting-comfort remarks [S5][S6] are not prevention policy, so -1 (not -2) at medium fits.

Not evidence on the reform axis as the rubric defines it (work within party/donor structures vs refuse PAC money, term limits, dark-money bans, RCV, direct democracy). Continuing Zempel's office approach [S5] is office continuity, already captured on experience; the dossier records no position on political money or structural reform.

25 years of prosecutorial and legal work [S1] but never in the county prosecutor's office and campaigning on a 'fresh slate, fresh eyes' [S4]; never held elected office [S1]. +1 rather than +2 correctly reflects the long legal record.

Pledges to 'aggressively prosecute violent and repeat offenders' [S1][S3] but adds concrete pre-filing diversion, cheaper treatment/diversion access for indigent defendants and recovery-navigator referrals for simple possession [S4][S5]. Mixed but prevention-leaning; +1 medium is right.

Not evidence on the reform axis as the rubric defines it (work within party/donor structures vs refuse PAC money, term limits, dark-money bans, RCV, direct democracy). The cited basis (reviewing what works, changing diversion handling [S4]) is office policy, scored on safety and experience. His independent, 'free from partisan politics' framing [S1][S4] is nonpartisan branding with no PAC-money, term-limit or similar plank, too thin even for low.
